messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 71-year-old insurance agent of North American ethnicity, has spent much of his life trying to navigate the shadows cast by childhood physical abuse inflicted upon him by a caregiver. John’s traumatic experiences have woven themselves deeply into the fabric of his daily existence, manifesting in complex ways that continue to affect his mental health and interpersonal relationships. John’s triggers are particularly potent, often activated by seemingly innocuous stimuli like talking to strangers or hearing sirens. The mere smell of alcohol can transport him back to those harrowing moments from his childhood, evoking vivid and distressing memories. These triggers have become so intertwined with his daily life that he has come to believe the people responsible for his trauma have faced no consequences, further intensifying his sense of betrayal and mistrust. When John encounters strangers in his line of work or even in casual settings, he feels an overwhelming sense of threat and unease, convinced that their approach is a harbinger of danger. This constant vigilance has led him to develop intrusive monitoring behaviors; he listens intently for any sounds that might indicate someone entering his home, constantly on edge as if expecting another attack. John’s memories of the traumatic event are fragmented but deeply real. They appear suddenly and vividly, often triggered by sensory cues like olfactory sensations reminiscent of those dark days. These memories feel more real than his ordinary experiences, which has led him to engage in various maladaptive strategies such as performing mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again. He keeps his mind occupied all the time, avoiding watching TV programs or reading books that might remind him of similar events. The vividness and realism of these memories have contributed to John’s heightened threat monitoring. When he feels threatened, it is not just by strangers; even false alarms—reacting as if in danger when nothing is actually wrong—add to his constant state of anxiety. This cycle has become a self-reinforcing loop where his negative appraisals exacerbate the triggers and vice versa. John’s body reacts as if he were still in danger, even though he knows logically that he is safe. He experiences this physiological response acutely, further fueling his sense of betrayal and mistrust. The constant need to monitor for threats has led him to avoid situations where he might encounter strangers or hear sirens, creating a cycle of avoidance and heightened anxiety. The maladaptive strategies John employs have also contributed significantly to his negative appraisals and ongoing threat monitoring. His efforts to distract himself mentally and perform rituals have only reinforced his belief that the world is inherently dangerous and unpredictable. This has led him to isolate himself further from social interactions, which once brought joy but now seem fraught with potential triggers. The interplay between these elements has taken a significant toll on John’s life. He has found it increasingly difficult to maintain relationships and perform his job as an insurance agent without the constant fear of encountering something that might trigger a traumatic memory or feeling of danger. It was this cumulative impact, coupled with growing isolation and a sense of hopelessness, that finally brought him to seek help. John is most afraid of not being able to control these overwhelming feelings and memories, but he also hopes for a way to break the cycle of fear and mistrust that has defined so much of his life. He seeks understanding and support in finding strategies that can alleviate the constant sense of threat and allow him to regain a sense of safety and normalcy in his daily experiences.
